scholarships.degree: Mostly Master's/PhD (a few UG-eligible programmes exist but are rare)
scholarships.description: DAAD (German Academic Exchange Service) is the world's largest funding organisation for international academic exchange. DAAD supports over 100,000 German and international students and researchers annually through 100+ individually funded programmes. DAAD scholarships do not have to be paid back. As of February 2026, the monthly stipend is EUR 992 for Master's students and EUR 1,400 for doctoral/PhD candidates. A flat-rate travel allowance is also provided. In many cases, DAAD also provides health, accident and personal liability insurance. Depending on the scholarship programme, there are also additional benefits such as a one-off research allowance, family benefits or funds for language courses. Not all DAAD programmes cover tuition - applicants must verify tuition coverage per individual programme on the DAAD Funding Guide database.

scholarships.title: Global Korea Scholarship (GKS)
scholarships.description: The Global Korea Scholarship (GKS), formerly known as the Korean Government Scholarship Program (KGSP), is offered by the Korean Government through the National Institute for International Education (NIIED). It supports international students for undergraduate (Bachelor's/Associate) studies in South Korea. The scholarship includes full tuition support, a monthly stipend, round-trip airfare, Korean language training (up to 1 year), settlement allowance, and medical insurance. There are two application tracks: (1) Embassy Track - apply through the Korean Embassy in the applicant's home country; (2) University Track - apply directly to a designated Korean university. The scholarship provides full tuition support, monthly living allowance, round-trip economy airfare, 1 year of Korean language training, settlement allowance, and medical insurance. Official details vary by track and cycle.

scholarships.title: MEXT (Monbukagakusho) Scholarship
scholarships.degree: UG/PG/PhD - separate application tracks: Undergraduate, Research Student (leads to Master's/PhD), Teacher Training, Japanese Studies, College of Technology
scholarships.description: The MEXT (Monbukagakusho) Scholarship is the Japanese Government Scholarship offered by the Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT). It supports international students for undergraduate, master's, and doctoral studies in Japan. Stipends vary by track: Undergraduate students receive JPY 117,000/month (per the 2027 undergraduate guideline); Research Students (Master's/PhD) receive JPY 148,000/month; Teacher Training and Japanese Studies students receive JPY 148,000/month; College of Technology students receive JPY 117,000/month. All tracks include full tuition, round-trip economy airfare, and 6 months to 1 year of Japanese language training. The scholarship is offered through multiple tracks: Research Student (leads to Master's/PhD), Undergraduate, Teacher Training, Japanese Studies, College of Technology, and Specialized Training College. There are two application paths for Bangladeshi applicants: (1) Embassy Recommendation - apply via Bangladesh Ministry of Education SHED portal, screened by Embassy of Japan Dhaka (written exam + interview); (2) University Recommendation - apply directly to a Japanese university which recommends to MEXT. Stipend rates per the 2027 MEXT guidelines; verify current rates at studyinjapan.go.jp.

scholarships.notes: Applications are reviewed by disciplinary and interdisciplinary scientists, engineers and STEM experts selected by NSF Program Officers, with care taken to ensure no conflicts of interest. Applications are reviewed in broad areas of related disciplines based on the Major Field of Study selected by the applicant, using the two NSF Merit Review Criteria: Intellectual Merit (potential to advance knowledge) and Broader Impacts (potential to benefit society and contribute to specific, desired societal outcomes). Intellectual Merit factors include the ability to plan and conduct research, work independently, work as part of a team, interpret and communicate research, take initiative, think creatively, solve problems, persist and overcome challenges, and demonstrated intellectual ability as indicated by grades, coursework and awards. Broader Impacts factors include increasing participation in STEM, improving STEM education through outreach and mentoring, increasing public scientific literacy, increasing collaboration among academia and industry, improving educator development, improving societal well-being, developing a globally competitive STEM workforce, improving national security, increasing U.S. economic competitiveness, and enhancing research and education infrastructure. GRFP was established to recruit and support individuals who demonstrate the potential to make significant contributions in STEM.

Following interviews, final selections are made at the discretion of the sponsoring federal agencies; finalists are contacted by ORISE regarding offers. DOE selects the finalists for Congressional office placements. All eligible and compliant applications are then reviewed externally by subject matter experts in the field of the proposed research, using the DOE Office of Science's standard merit review processes. Two merit review criteria apply: (1) Scientific and/or Technical Merit of the Proposed Research, asking whether the research is well-conceived with a clear understanding of the scientific and technical challenges, whether the method and approach are appropriate, whether the graduate student is sufficiently well prepared, and whether DOE laboratory resources are adequate, including whether necessary access to a scientific user facility has been secured by the collaborating scientist; and (2) Relevance of the Proposed Research to Graduate Thesis Research and Training, asking whether the proposed research can make a significant contribution to the applicant's thesis project and whether it will enhance the applicant's graduate training and research skills. Applications are selected for award based on the results of peer review and other program policy factors, including availability of funds and balance of portfolio. The application materials received, including the research proposal, provide the sole basis for evaluation. Participation in other DOE programmes is collected for internal purposes only and does not affect selection.

The committee produces (1) a list of projects it recommends for funding on the published criteria and (2) a list it proposes not to fund because quality is insufficient on at least one criterion, with a written justification for each project, and may give an opinion on the amount requested. Uninvolved PEPR GFM programme directors then propose to the SGPI which projects could be financed and at what amount; the Prime Minister, after opinion of the CPMo and the SGPI, decides beneficiaries and amounts, and each project is covered by a contract between the ANR and the coordinating institution. Evaluation criteria fall into three groups: (a) scientific ambition and excellence (research question going beyond the documented state of the art, discipline combination justified by the question, dialogue of conceptual frameworks, ethical questions treated as integral to ambition); (b) quality of the consortium, resources mobilised and governance (recognised complementary expertise, adequacy of staff with objectives including a precise role and career benefit for each contractual worker, structured maturation phase, mechanisms for shared appropriation of questions, inventory/acquisition/management strategy for data and samples, recurrent ethical monitoring mechanisms, explicit choices to minimise the environmental footprint, coherent sizing with an argued 0.8-3 M€ budget); (c) fit with the PEPR GFM challenges and impact (clear fit with at least one challenge and the programme's strategic priorities, described scientific/economic/environmental/societal impacts, described sharing of data and results, open-access data strategy with FAIR and CARE and Opidor PGD links, dissemination to academic and non-academic audiences).

Evaluation criteria fall into three groups: (1) excellence and scientific ambition in precision psychiatry - clarity of objectives and hypotheses, innovativeness, ambition, originality, methodological or conceptual rupture against the state of the art, methodological relevance, preliminary data, project feasibility; (2) quality of the consortium, project management, resources mobilised and governance - competence, expertise and involvement of the project leader including capacity to coordinate ambitious multidisciplinary projects or consortia, academic track record, international recognition, quality and complementarity of the scientific consortium, adequacy between human and financial means and the objectives, relevance of the schedule and management of scientific risks with alternative solutions and credible milestones, relevance and efficiency of governance including patient associations and links with industrial partners or other programmes; (3) impact and outcomes - capacity to address precision-psychiatry development issues, active strategy to measure economic and/or societal impact, contribution to solutions for pathophysiological, diagnostic or therapeutic issues, dissemination and valorization strategy in itinere and ex post, adherence to FAIR and Open Science principles and promotion of scientific culture.
